summary: Coast Guard light at the end of the Cedar Point jetty in Sandusky Bay; the permanent light was lit in 1928 and a 1933 jetty rescue is on record.

structures.note: Twenty-foot (6.1 m) steel skeletal tower with a square lantern room (LighthouseFriends); replaced by the current tower in the mid-1990s.
Current tower, which replaced the 1925 tower in the mid-1990s (LighthouseFriends).

staffing.note: Remotely controlled by cable from Cedar Point (LighthouseFriends).

access.note: Coast Guard property. The tower is closed.

events.note: Act of 17 June 1910 authorized a light and fog signal at the entrance to Sandusky Bay; no appropriation had been made as of the 1920 report.
Nearly 5,000-foot jetty completed in 1914; it stayed unmarked until an appropriation (LighthouseFriends).
Lighthouse Service Bulletin lists a Sandusky Pierhead light, flashing white with an acetylene lantern, as established. LighthouseFriends dates the first light to 1925-1928. Conflict; see notes.
Steel tower fabricated at the Buffalo depot and erected on a concrete foundation at the jetty's outer end (LighthouseFriends).
About ten men from Cleveland, with more than 100 fishermen on the jetty, were taken off the locked lantern room by the Coast Guard after a northeaster (LighthouseFriends, citing the Star Journal).

corrections.why: The record lists the 1925 tower as standing. LighthouseFriends says it was replaced by the current tower in the mid-1990s.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The light is called Sandusky Pierhead Light in the Lighthouse Service's 1921 list and in LighthouseFriends, and Sandusky Harbor Breakwater Light in the record. The story uses the record's English name and gives the other in the text.

notes_for_editor: (1) First light: the record gives 1925 (from Wikidata and Rowlett). The 1921 Bulletin lists a Sandusky Pierhead light, flashing white with a lens lantern and acetylene, as established, and the 1918-1923 Bulletin index has 'Sandusky Pierhead light established' (PDF page 34). LighthouseFriends says a temporary acetylene light was shown from the 1925 tower until the permanent light on 15 March 1928. Unresolved. The Commissioner's reports for 1924 to 1928 are not in the local corpus; check them. (2) Characteristic: the record gives Fl W 6s (ENC and OSM) and Fl W 4s (Wikidata). LighthouseFriends gives the 1928 pattern as four seconds of white and a two-second eclipse, which is not a flash. The present characteristic needs the current Light List. (3) Focal height and range: the record has 9.1 m and 9 nm. LighthouseFriends gives a 66-foot (20.1 m) focal plane and says the light could be seen for up to fifteen miles, without saying statute or nautical miles. The facts object therefore carries the focal height only; the range was removed rather than converted. (4) Structure: the record lists the 1925 tower as standing; LighthouseFriends says it was replaced in the mid-1990s (a correction is proposed). The record's 1990 date for 'Tower 2' comes from Rowlett and I did not confirm it in a text I read. (5) No keeper roster: the USLHS place match failed for this breakwater light. LighthouseFriends says it was controlled from Cedar Point, where keepers of the range lights lived; no keeper is named for this light in the sources read. (6) The 1933 rescue is second-hand: LighthouseFriends quotes the Star Journal of 5 July 1933. The newspaper search returned no Ohio hits for that date. The 1933 men are not named here. (7) Checked on the page image of the 1938 Bulletin (PDF page 2): the sentence 'Among the more important projects were the light stations at Oswego, Rochester, and Buffalo ... Lorain, and Sandusky, in Ohio' belongs to the reconstruction programme carried out in the Tenth District since 1910. The 1933-1936 programme is given only as about 25 projects at roughly $500,000, with no names, so the story does not place Sandusky in it. An earlier version of the record tied Sandusky to the 1933-1936 programme; that event was removed. (8) The USCG Historian's pages for this light could not be read: the archived copies I tried returned 404. (9) Only one secondary history and three Bulletin or Commissioner passages were read. The 1920 note also says the Engineer Department had an appropriation for the pierhead's underwater part, which the story now states. The story is short on purpose. Photos were not added.
